content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
The authors establish a new bound on the spectrum associated with a quantum kernel, in terms of a bandwidth parameter recommended for use in earlier work.  This leads to a new generalization upper bound, which is consistent with the previous observation that the bandwidth parameter could be used to improve generalization in practice.  

The consensus view that emerged was that this paper did not have enough fundamentally novel content for publication in ICLR.

content.title: Response to Reviewer YWYZ Part 2/2
content.comment:
2. As the reviewer pointed out, our theoretical analysis relies on the toy kernel introduced in Eq. 6 for regression tasks, while the numerical experiments presented in Section 4.2 were performed on realistic quantum kernels for binary classification tasks.

    First, we would like to note that the central goal of this work is to explain the behavior of real quantum kernels on real data as observed in Shaydulin & Wild, 2021. To explain these numerical results and provide a mathematical mechanism by which bandwidth enables generalization, we derive the analytical results in Section 4.1. However, in either classical or quantum settings, restrictive assumptions must be placed on the kernel to derive the analytical kernel spectrum in closed form. At the same time, studying these simple kernels provides an intuition and tests a mathematical framework for understanding the behavior of more interesting and relevant data distributions. Therefore, theoretical results in Section 4.1 use an analytically tractable kernel that is available in closed form, which is different from the more general quantum kernels studied in Section 4.2.

    Despite the differences in the settings chosen for theoretical and numerical analysis, the intuition developed in Section 4.1 applies to more general kernels. Specifically, we observe the same behavior (bandwidth tuning improves the spectrum and task-model alignment) for quantum kernels not available in closed form (e.g. the IQP kernel; see Figure 3) as we do for the analytically tractable kernel considered in Section 4.1. The fact that the same behavior is observed for kernels and data far outside our theoretical assumptions only reinforces the power of the developed framework.

    Finally, we understand that using our theory on regression tasks to explain the generalization phenomena in a classification task can be confusing. However, we note that regression and binary classification are related to each other. Denoting $\psi(\mathbf{x}^\mu)$ as the feature vector corresponding to sample $\mathbf{x}^\mu$, and $y^\mu \in \\{-1, 1\\}$ as the binary labels, the goal of a regression task is to find weights $\mathbf{w}$ such that $\mathbf{w}\cdot \psi(\mathbf{x}^\mu) \approx y^\mu$ for all training samples, while in the classification the task is to get the correct sign for all training samples: $\text{sign}\left(\mathbf{w}\cdot \psi(\mathbf{x}^\mu)\right) = y^\mu$. Therefore, the classification task can be considered as a simpler problem, hence we expect our intuitions from our theory to hold. Nevertheless, for completeness, we performed regression on the same dataset and reported the test loss for varying bandwidth hyperparameters under Appendix E.2. As expected, the test loss is the smallest when the bandwidth is tuned, and it is consistent with our SVM results.

**Clarity, Quality, Novelty And Reproducibility**

We thank the reviewer for the feedback on the layout of tables and figures. We will improve our main text regarding the readability of our paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer YWYZ Part 1/2
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful assessments and for pointing out the concerns regarding novelty and the alignment between theory and numerical experiments. In this response, we address both concerns in detail. Based on the clarifications below, we kindly ask the reviewer to reconsider the score.

**Weakness**

1. We thank the reviewer for raising concerns regarding the novelty of using bandwidth to improve generalization. We are aware that bandwidth is an old and well known concept, however in this paper we argue that bandwidth scaling of inputs is required for quantum kernels simply due to its intrinsic exponential dimensionality. We believe that the significance of this dimensionality problem, which remains unsolved despite being characterized in a large body of quantum machine learning literature  (e.g. Refs [1-5] ), justifies our exploration of techniques involving bandwidth that might otherwise be well known in classical machine learning literature.
    
    Note that unlike classical kernels such as Gaussian RBF that must be optimally chosen via cross validation, bandwidth does not explicitly appear as a hyperparameter for the quantum kernel. The quantum kernels we consider are constructed by transforming qubits by unitary operations which parametrically depend on the inputs. For example, a single qubit $\alpha \left| 0 \right\rangle + \beta \left| 1 \right\rangle$ satisfying $|\alpha|^2 + |\beta|^2 = 1$ can be phase rotated to $\alpha \left| 0 \right\rangle + \beta e^{2\pi i x} \left| 1 \right\rangle$ depending on a single scalar input $x$. Standard quantum computations are performed by such operations acting on a state space which is exponentially large in number of qubits and can be provably more advantageous for certain problems compared to their classical counterparts. 

    The idea behind quantum kernels is exploiting such rich state spaces for machine learning applications. In this case, these kernels correspond to exponentially large feature spaces which have more representational power compared to their classical counterparts. However, this expressive power comes at a cost, the large volume of possible solutions make learning exponentially hard in terms of sample complexity. Hence, naively creating kernels out of such quantum feature maps makes learning impossible with polynomial amount of samples. This is the reason why we introduce bandwidth by hand through scaling inputs, which we prove, using a toy model, restricts the effective dimensionality of the feature space and hence enables generalization. As we noted in the manuscript, there may be other techniques which can induce such an effect, however bandwidth is the simplest one which had not been studied in the context of quantum kernels.
    
    For clarification, we would also like to note that a provable advantage of such quantum representations over classical counterparts remains to be seen, and we do not claim that quantum feature spaces have *better* expressive power over classical kernels. However, our claim is that if such advantages were to be found, one still needs to restrict the quantum feature space in order to enable learning in polynomial time.

[1] McClean, J.R., Boixo, S., Smelyanskiy, V.N. et al. Barren plateaus in quantum neural network training landscapes. Nat Commun 9, 4812 (2018).

[2] Cerezo, M., Sone, A., Volkoff, T. et al. Cost function dependent barren plateaus in shallow parametrized quantum circuits. Nat Commun 12, 1791 (2021).

[3] Wang, S., Fontana, E., Cerezo, M. et al. Noise-induced barren plateaus in variational quantum algorithms. Nat Commun 12, 6961 (2021).

[4] Holmes, Z., Sharma, K., Cerezo, M., & Coles, P. J. Connecting ansatz expressibility to gradient magnitudes and barren plateaus. PRX Quantum, 3(1), 010313 (2022). 

[5] Thanasilp, S., Wang, S., Cerezo, M., & Holmes, Z. Exponential concentration and untrainability in quantum kernel methods. arXiv:2208.11060 (2022).

content.title: Response to Reviewer em9T
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the positive assessment of our work and a detailed review. We address the questions raised by the reviewer below.

**Strength And Weaknesses**

As the reviewer pointed out, our main theoretical analysis is based on a simplistic quantum kernel which enables theoretical analysis since it can be expressed in closed form. Our main goal in this paper is to provide intuition and the mathematical mechanisms by which quantum kernels may generalize through bandwidth. We do so using a toy model and test if our intuitions hold for more realistic quantum kernels which do not have closed form expressions and cannot be treated as explicitly as we do on our toy model.

**Clarity, Quality, Novelty And Reproducibility**

We thank the reviewer for pointing out the clarity issues and typos. We have made the suggested changes and below provide answers for the reviewer's questions.

- In our notation, $\bar y^\mu$ denotes the $\mu^\text{th}$ training label and $\bar{\mathbf{y}}$  denotes the vector of all labels whose $\mu^\text{th}$ element is $\bar y^\mu$.
- Thank you for pointing out that the explanation of Bloch sphere is unclear. In the said line, we added 
 >>the density matrix can be written in terms of Pauli matrices $\vec{\sigma}$ as $\rho = \frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \mathbf{n}\cdot\vec{\sigma}\right)$.
- In our notation, $\psi(\mathbf{x})$ denotes a generic feature map for some machine learning model. For quantum kernels, the density matrix $\rho(\mathbf{x})$ is associated with the feature map of the quantum machine learning model. Hence, we use the density matrix which maps inputs $\mathbf{x}$ to a feature matrix $\rho(\mathbf{x})$ of size $2^n\times 2^n$. For clarity, we changed the expression to $\psi(\mathbf{x}) = \rho(\mathbf{x})$.

content.title: Response to Reviewer jwdc
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for careful assessments and comments. In the following, we answer the reviewer's questions.

**Summary Of The Paper**

Indeed, as the reviewer correctly stated, the eigenvalues of the quantum kernels are exponentially small in number of qubits, which reflects the fact that there are no spectral biases to aid learning. While the quantum kernels are potentially more expressive than classical kernels, learning with these kernels require exponentially many samples. However, as previously observed in the data by Shaydulin & Wild (2021), rescaling the inputs via the bandwidth hyperparameter enables generalization with reasonable amount of data. The main goal of this paper is to explain this observation mathematically using a toy quantum kernel and show that our intuitions transfer to the more realistic quantum kernels.  

Below, we answer the questions raised by the reviewer:

- In quantum machine learning, one first needs to encode the data in qubits to process, so indeed the number of qubits must be at least $n$, the dimension of data. For example, we apply PCA to our data for reducing the data dimension from $784$ to $22$ ($2^{22}$ dimensional Hilbert space) to be able to perform quantum simulation experiments with currently available computational resources.
- Indeed, the kernel in Eq. 5 can be classically solved and we presented experiments on this kernel in Fig. 1 and Fig. 2. While this kernel is obtained by quantum operations, it does not have entanglement and does not take advantage of whole $2^n$ dimensional feature space (qubits do not couple and can be treated independently.) This is why it can be written analytically, solved classically and used for theoretical analysis. On the other hand, entangled quantum kernels do not have analytically closed forms and should be evaluated either through simulations which are computationally expensive or using quantum computers.
- The kernels were pre-computed by quantum simulations with a grid search on bandwidth parameters in Shaydulin & Wild (2021), and the dataset provided includes kernels for a variety of bandwidth parameters. For our theoretical analysis, we also needed to study the kernel spectrum for suboptimal bandwidth parameters in order to analyze the scaling of the bandwidth as a function of number of qubits (Fig. A.5, A.6 and A.7).

**Strength And Weaknesses**

The main message we want to convey is that the quantum kernel models could be promising due to their computational and representational power, however harnessing their potential in machine learning requires imposing spectral biases by hand, since these models have very poor inductive biases. We impose such spectral bias constraints using the bandwidth parameter and show how this helps generalization. We derive the optimal bandwidth parameter as a function of number of qubits for our toy model, and empirically show that similar scaling laws hold for more realistic quantum kernels.

content.title: Response to Reviewer P99u
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for pointing out the concerns regarding the novelty. In the following, we answer to the reviewer's comments. With the following clarifications in mind, we kindly ask the reviewer to reconsider the score.

**Strength And Weaknesses**

We kindly point out that while the idea of bandwidth for quantum kernel has indeed appeared in (Shaydulin & Wild, 2021), said reference contains only numerical evidence and no explanation for the observed behavior.

The novelty of the current work is that we provide the mathematical mechanism explaining how bandwidth improves the generalization of quantum kernels. Specifically, we derive novel formulas for the spectrum of a bandwidth-equipped quantum kernel, which we then use in conjunction with the task-model alignment framework of (Canatar et al., 2021) to derive the optimal scaling of the bandwidth parameter with the number of qubits. 

While we cannot apply similar analysis to the more realistic kernels studied in Section 4.2 since they do not have closed form expressions, we emprically show that these kernels too obey a similar scaling law for the bandwidth (see Appendix E.2).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studied the failure of the generalization of the quantum kernel method by focusing on the major cosine kernel function. The authors proposed introducing the bandwidth to control the spectrum of the cosine kernel. The authors derived the formula of the spectrum for that kernel. Then the authors showed that introducing the bandwidth improves the generalization by combining the generalization error bound of the existing work and deriving the spectrum formula.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strength
- The authors rigorously evaluated the eigenvalues of cosine kernel under the large qubit settings and showed how the bandwidth affects the spectrum. Then the authors also derived the scaling laws of the spectrum. As far as I know, the derived scaling laws are new and meaningful.
- Combined with the spectrum, the authors derived the generalization error of the kernel regression task and showed that introducing the bandwidth improves the generalization. 

# Weakness
- The idea of using bandwidth is not new.
- The generalization analysis is not novel; it just substitutes the derived spectrum formula into the Theorem in Canatar 2021.
- The analysis and numerical experiments are not consistent. The generalization analysis focuses on the regression task, but numerical experiments are the classification task. Also, the authors used different kernel functions from the theoretical analysis. Thus, it is hard to judge how significant the theoretical analysis is in a real-world application.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I think the layout of tables and figures should be improved. For example, the caption of Table 2 and Figure 3 are hard to distinguish from the main text.
content.summary_of_the_review: As I wrote in the weakness, the contribution of this paper is not significant and novel. Using the bandwidth is not new and the derived generalization error bound is the simple application of existing work. The derived scaling law of the spectrum seems new and interesting, but the numerical experiments are conducted with different kernel functions from the theory; thus hard to see the usefulness of the theoretical analysis.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Prior works have shown that quantum kernel methods may not generalize well on machine learning tasks because the spectrum of the kernel operator is too flat. This work shows that by tuning an appropriate bandwidth parameter in the kernel, the spectrum can be made less flat, hence enabling generalization.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is very well-written with clear, intuitive explanations, and gives compelling reasoning for the use of bandwidth in quantum kernels.

The main weakness of the work is that the theoretical results are very specific, pertaining to a specific kernel, and the analysis seems hard to generalize to more realistic kernels; also, the result is not a fully rigorous analysis of the generalization error. Nevertheless I believe that addressing these issues is best left as future work, and the current paper already makes a solid contribution by providing elucidating intuition.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is very clear and of high quality. The novelty of the paper is not that high, since the idea of using bandwidth has appeared in prior literature, but the spectral analysis in this paper is to the best of my knowledge new. I have hardly found any typos which is impressive, but I point out some suggestions for clarity:
- The ICLR submission title has a typo “bandwith”
- On pg. 2 near the top, “show that the generalization is impossible” should be changed to “show that generalization is impossible”
- On pg. 3, what is the meaning of the equation $\bar{\mathbf y}_\mu = \bar y^\mu$? Namely, why are there bars?
- On pg. 3, the explanation of the Bloch sphere is hard to understand without explicitly writing out the parameterization of the density matrix in terms of n.
- Pg. 3, what is the meaning of $\psi(\mathbf x) \to \rho(\mathbf x)$?
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the analysis in this work should be viewed as preliminary and awaits more detailed study, nevertheless I found the submission to be illuminating and well-written, and hence I recommend acceptance.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper studies quantum kernel learning. Their observation seems that the dimension of the feature maps associated with quantum kernels is exponential but can be processed by quantum boxes. The problem with these kernel is that their leading eigenvalues are too small so that these models do not generalize well. The authors then observe that if one change the ``bandwidth’’ of these kernel functions, then distribution of the eigenvalues becomes more benign. I am not sure whether I interpret the result correctly, but it appears that the authors provide analysis for one specific kernel (with closed forms) and argued that tuning bandwidth could be beneficial for other kernels. 

The paper is quite well written and provided careful exposition to both kernel learning and quantum computing (I was able to follow more than 50% of the paper). The results also appear to be quite significant, especially in a new area. I am leaning towards acceptance.


Is the number of cubits needed the same as the dimension of the data? That sounds quite painful? 
For the problem analyzed (eq. 5), because the kernel can be explicitly written, what’s the reason that this kernel cannot be solved by classical computers? 
In the experiment, it was stated that pre-computed kernels are used. But if kernel bandwidth needs to be tuned, wouldn’t that just mean pre-computed values could be mostly irrelevant?
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: the paper gave a quite clear exposition to quantum kernel learning and the paper’s result appears to be quite significant. 


Weakness: I am still not sure about whether I understand the big picture (perhaps just me not knowing enough about quantum). See the questions above.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Mostly clear; 
but quantum is still too foreign to me.

(+) it gives a fairly reasonable overview of quantum kernel learning. 
(+) it appears to be a significant result for quantum kernel learning. 

(-) Probably most people in iclr wont understand quantum part. 
(-) I cannot calibrate the technical depth of the result.

content.title: Bandwith Enables Generalization in Quantum Kernel Models
content.abstract: Quantum computers are known to provide speedups over classical state-of-the-art machine learning methods in some specialized settings. For example, quantum kernel methods have been shown to provide an exponential speedup on a learning version of the discrete logarithm problem. Understanding the generalization of quantum models is essential to realizing similar speedups on practically interesting problems. Recent results demonstrate that generalization is hindered by the exponential size of the quantum feature space. Although these results suggest that quantum models cannot generalize when the number of qubits is large, in this paper we show that these results rely on overly restrictive assumptions. We consider a wider class of models by varying a hyperparameter that we call quantum kernel bandwidth. We analyze the large-qubit limit and provide explicit formulas for the generalization of a quantum model that can be solved in closed form. Specifically, we show that changing the value of bandwidth can take a model from provably not being able to generalize on any target function to good generalization for well-aligned targets. Our analysis shows how the bandwidth controls the spectrum of the kernel integral operator, and thereby the inductive bias of the model. We demonstrate empirically that our theory correctly predicts how varying the bandwidth affects generalization of quantum models on challenging datasets, including those far outside our theoretical assumptions. We discuss the implications of our results for quantum advantage in machine learning.
